lessons.summary: Design focused inquiries that connect spatial, historical, economic and social evidence.
objectives: Turn a broad theme into a focused question.
Choose evidence suited to the question.
Synthesize more than one disciplinary lens.
keyIdeas: A strong inquiry names a relationship, context and workable scope.
Different disciplines make different evidence visible.
Synthesis explains what the combined view reveals.

definitions.meaning: A focused, researchable question that guides evidence collection and reasoning.
The boundaries of place, time, population and concept used in an inquiry.
An integrated explanation built from multiple sources or disciplinary perspectives.

method: Name the issue and possible relationship.
Bound it by place, time and population.
Check that evidence could challenge the expected answer.
Select at least two disciplinary lenses and explain their contribution.

steps: Define location and time.
Replace “good” with measurable social, economic and environmental effects.
Allow competing outcomes.
workedExample.conclusion: A stronger question is: “To what extent did increased tourism from 2018 to 2025 change employment and coastal habitat quality in Region X?”

misconceptions.mistake: Writing a question that contains its desired conclusion.
misconceptions.correction: Use wording that permits evidence to support, weaken or complicate the claim.
Set the boundaries first so evidence can be selected deliberately.

practice.prompt: Turn “pollution in cities” into a focused inquiry question.
hints: Add a city, time period, pollutant and affected outcome.
solution: Example: “How did roadside nitrogen dioxide levels relate to childhood asthma admissions in City X from 2020 to 2025?”

practice.prompt: Justify two source types for investigating a new transport policy.
hints: Connect each source to a different part of the question.
solution: Traffic-count data can show movement changes.
Resident interviews can reveal unequal access or lived effects.
Together they compare measured patterns with experience.

practice.prompt: Evaluate whether economic growth alone can measure a redevelopment project’s success.
hints: Bring in spatial and social evidence.
solution: Growth can show investment or income change but may hide distribution.
Displacement, travel access, housing cost and environmental quality may move differently.
A defensible evaluation needs multiple indicators and stakeholder evidence.

practice.prompt: Turn the fictional topic “school travel” into a focused descriptive question with a place, period and measurable outcome.
hints: Choose one travel measure.
Bound the population and dates.
solution: Possible answer: What proportion of pupils at School A walked to school during the first week of October?
This identifies a population, interval and measurable mode share without claiming a cause.

practice.prompt: An inquiry defines successful redevelopment only after seeing that shop sales rose but rents also rose. What problem arises and how can it be improved?
hints: Criteria may be chosen to favour the result.
Use explicit criteria and explain any revisions.
solution: Selecting success criteria after seeing results can privilege the favourable outcome.
Specify sales, affordability and other justified criteria transparently, and report how each changed rather than concealing the rent trade-off.

checklist: My question is focused and contestable.
My evidence can test the claim.
I synthesize rather than place disciplines side by side.

notes.title: A broad idea becomes a measurable inquiry
paragraphs: An inquiry question becomes manageable when it names a place, a period, an outcome and a comparison. Descriptive questions establish what changed; explanatory questions examine why; evaluative questions judge change against explicit criteria. These forms can support one another, but they require different evidence. Define terms such as accessible or successful before collecting data so the judgement is not adjusted to fit a preferred result. A feasible inquiry also considers source availability and whose experiences may be missing. Narrowing the question should improve the match between claim and evidence without excluding inconvenient groups.

workedExamples.prompt: Refine the fictional topic “parks and wellbeing” into a feasible local inquiry using a stated six-month project period.
steps: Choose an observable outcome such as park visits and a defined group, such as residents of two named neighbourhoods.
Possible question: How did weekly park use among surveyed residents of East and West neighbourhoods change during the six months after new paths opened?
workedExamples.conclusion: The question measures use; it does not automatically measure all dimensions of wellbeing.

flashcards.front: What does a descriptive inquiry ask?
flashcards.back: What happened or what pattern exists.

flashcards.front: What does an explanatory inquiry ask?
flashcards.back: Why or through what mechanism a pattern occurred.

flashcards.front: What makes an evaluative inquiry explicit?
flashcards.back: Named criteria for judging success or value.

flashcards.front: Why define key terms early?
flashcards.back: To make evidence collection and judgement consistent.

diagrams.title: A broad idea becomes a measurable inquiry
diagrams.description: The outcome must fit the claim being investigated.

nodes.label: Defined outcome
nodes.detail: Weekly park use in two neighbourhoods

nodes.label: Bounded question
nodes.detail: Change over six months after paths opened

edges.label: select an observable part of the topic

lessons.summary: Interrogate evidence through historical, geographical and economic lenses, then synthesize what the combined reading can and cannot establish.
objectives: Distinguish observation, inference and claim.
Evaluate provenance in relation to a specific inquiry.
Synthesize evidence from different disciplines without flattening their differences.
keyIdeas: A source is useful for a purpose, not reliable in the abstract.
Maps, statistics, testimony and policy texts make different features visible.
Synthesis explains how evidence changes when two disciplinary readings are combined.

definitions.meaning: Who created a source, when, where, for whom and for what purpose.
Testing a claim by comparing it with independent evidence.
The spatial, temporal or analytical level at which evidence is collected and interpreted.

method: State the inquiry before judging the source.
Separate what the source directly shows from what you infer.
Connect origin, purpose and method to a precise value or limitation.
Corroborate with a source that could reveal a different pattern or challenge the claim.
Synthesize agreements, tensions and remaining uncertainty.

workedExample.prompt: A city report says a transport project reduced average journey time by 12%. A neighbourhood interview study reports longer trips for some residents. How should the evidence be combined?
steps: The city statistic gives a system-wide average but may hide variation.
The interviews reveal lived effects and possible distributional differences but may cover a small sample.
Check route, neighbourhood, time period and measurement method in both sources.
Seek disaggregated travel-time data to test whether the reported experiences form a wider pattern.
workedExample.conclusion: The sources need not contradict each other: the average may improve while particular groups experience worse journeys.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling a source biased and therefore useless.
misconceptions.correction: Explain how purpose or selection affects its value for this particular inquiry.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating two agreeing sources as independent confirmation.
misconceptions.correction: Check whether they rely on the same original dataset, author or institution.

practice.prompt: Distinguish an observation from an inference using a photograph of a crowded railway platform.
hints: State what is directly visible before explaining it.
solution: Observation: many people are standing close together on the platform.
Inference: demand may be high or a service may be delayed.
The photograph alone does not establish why the crowd formed.

practice.prompt: Explain one value and one limitation of a business survey for investigating the effect of a new pedestrian zone.
hints: Tie each point to the inquiry and survey method.
solution: The survey can reveal how sampled owners report changes in footfall, costs or sales.
Self-reported change may be affected by recall, expectations or which businesses responded.
Transaction data and pedestrian counts could test the reported pattern.

practice.prompt: A flood map shows expanding high-risk zones while oral histories describe fewer damaging floods. Synthesize the evidence.
hints: Consider scale, protection and the difference between hazard and impact.
solution: The map may show rising physical exposure.
Flood defences, warnings or household adaptation may reduce experienced damage.
Oral histories can miss rare events or differ by location.
A synthesis should compare mapped hazard, protection measures and dated loss records before concluding.

practice.prompt: A fictional library reports 400 visits but only 250 registered visitors in a week. Give a coherent interpretation without assuming an error.
hints: Visits and distinct visitors are different units.
Some people may return.
solution: A visitor can make several visits during the week.
Thus 250 people can account for 400 visits; the definitions should be checked before alleging inconsistency.

practice.prompt: A fictional resident interview describes a long commute, while a city report gives a short mean commute. Does one necessarily disprove the other?
hints: An average can contain long and short journeys.
Check population and timing.
solution: One long commute can coexist with a short citywide mean.
Compare the resident’s circumstances and the report’s coverage; the interview may reveal uneven experiences hidden by the average.

checklist: I corroborate with genuinely independent evidence.

notes.title: Different counting units can coexist
paragraphs: Interdisciplinary sources may use different units of observation. A transport survey might describe individual journeys, an administrative report might describe annual totals and an interview might explain one person’s experience. These sources need not agree numerically to be useful together. First align dates, boundaries and definitions; then identify whether the disagreement is factual or reflects different scales. Quantitative summaries reveal patterns, while qualitative accounts can suggest mechanisms and overlooked outcomes. Neither form automatically outranks the other. Claims should retain the source’s scope and distinguish what was directly recorded from the interpretation built upon it.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional packet: a bus report shows 1000 boardings per day; a survey identifies 600 distinct daily riders. Explain why the figures need not conflict.
steps: Boardings count journeys onto buses, while distinct riders count people.
One person can board more than once, so 1000 boardings can be made by 600 people.
workedExamples.conclusion: Compare definitions before treating the difference as an error.

flashcards.front: What is a unit of observation?
flashcards.back: The entity counted or measured, such as a person or journey.

flashcards.front: Why align dates and boundaries?
flashcards.back: Different coverage can create apparent disagreement.

flashcards.front: What can interviews add?
flashcards.back: Detailed experience and possible mechanisms.

flashcards.front: Does a numerical source automatically outrank testimony?
flashcards.back: No; usefulness depends on the question and method.

diagrams.title: Different counting units can coexist
diagrams.description: A person can contribute several journeys to a transport total.

nodes.label: Repeated journeys
nodes.detail: Some riders board more than once

lessons.summary: Describe spatial differences using suitable rates and scale, then test explanations without inferring individual outcomes.
objectives: Distinguish location, pattern and explanation.
Calculate comparable rates for differently sized populations.
Evaluate how boundaries and aggregation affect a claim.
explanation: A spatial pattern describes how a measured feature varies across places. Identify the area, date, units and classification before describing concentrations, contrasts or exceptions. Raw counts can reflect differences in population size rather than differences in prevalence. A rate compares a count with a relevant population or exposure denominator. Use the same definitions and period for each place, and state what the denominator represents.

Historical and economic evidence can help explain a pattern, but a map alone rarely isolates a cause. Past investment, land use and current affordability may each be relevant; treat them as hypotheses until supported. Changing district boundaries can change averages without anyone moving. District-level patterns also need not describe every resident. The hypothetical cases below require a description first, then a qualified explanation and a clear proposal for evidence that could challenge it.
keyIdeas: Rates require a relevant denominator.
Scale affects visible patterns.
A spatial association is not a complete causal explanation.

definitions.meaning: The distribution of a measured feature across locations.
A quantity expressed relative to a relevant denominator over a specified scope or interval.
Combining observations into groups or areas, which can conceal variation within them.

method: Read place, period, boundaries and measurement definitions.
Choose a count or rate suited to the question.
Describe the contrast using specific evidence.
Test possible explanations with historical, economic and finer-scale evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical districts, measured in the same year and with the same definition: A has 200 households without a library card out of 1,000; B has 300 out of 3,000. Compare counts and proportions.
steps: B has the larger count: 300 compared with 200 households.
A has twice B’s proportion, despite the smaller count. A library card is not proof of library use or convenient access.
workedExample.conclusion: Use counts for the number affected and proportions for prevalence. Neither measure alone explains the difference.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling the largest count the highest prevalence.
Treating a district average as every resident’s situation.
misconceptions.correction: Examine variation within districts and avoid individual claims without individual data.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical districts use the same definition of a long commute: A has 60 of 400 surveyed residents above the threshold; B has 90 of 900. Calculate both sample proportions.
hints: Use each sample’s own denominator.
solution: These describe the samples; population generalisation depends on sampling.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical town has an average journey time of 25 minutes. A report concludes that every resident takes 25 minutes to travel. Explain the error and propose a better description.
hints: An average summarises a distribution.
solution: Different journey times can produce the same average of 25 minutes.
Report the spread and relevant neighbourhood or traveller groups alongside the mean.
Individual journey times are needed to describe each resident.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical map shows more empty shops in districts with higher rents. Evaluate the claim that rent alone caused every vacancy.
hints: What else could shape both measures?
solution: The map shows a district-level association under its definitions.
Footfall, local incomes, building conditions or changing demand could contribute.
Comparable rent histories, vacancy timing and evidence on alternative causes are needed to assess the rent mechanism; the map alone cannot attribute every vacancy.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical districts have 10 parks across 5 km² and 12 parks across 12 km². Compare park counts and densities.
hints: Divide parks by area.
Counts and density answer different questions.
solution: The first has 2 parks/km²; the second has 1 park/km².
The second has more parks in total, but the first has higher park density.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical map shows low shop occupancy near an old industrial zone. A report attributes every vacancy to distance from the centre. Identify a limitation and useful evidence.
hints: Other location-linked factors may vary.
Test the proposed distance mechanism.
solution: Building condition, rents or transport access could also explain the cluster.
Compare similar properties at different distances and examine these factors before assigning every vacancy to distance alone.

notes.title: Aggregation can conceal neighbourhood contrast
paragraphs: Spatial patterns depend on the scale and boundaries used to summarise data. A citywide average can conceal neighbourhood clusters, while small-area figures can vary sharply when populations are small. Compare counts with rates and inspect denominators before interpreting a map. Nearby places may share infrastructure, environmental conditions or historical development, so spatial association does not identify one cause. Aggregating districts can also change the visible pattern without changing any individual observation. A useful interpretation states where a pattern appears, how strong it is in the supplied data and what additional evidence could test the proposed explanation.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical neighbourhoods: North has 80 bus users among 100 surveyed residents; South has 20 among 100. Find the combined share and explain what it hides.
steps: Combined bus users = 100 of 200, giving 50%.
The average hides the contrast between North’s 80% and South’s 20%.
workedExamples.conclusion: A citywide 50% share does not describe either neighbourhood’s local rate.

flashcards.front: What can aggregation hide?
flashcards.back: Local differences and clusters.

flashcards.front: Why inspect denominators?
flashcards.back: Small samples can produce unstable-looking rates.

flashcards.front: Does a spatial correlation prove one cause?
flashcards.back: No; several shared influences may operate.

flashcards.front: What should a pattern description include?
flashcards.back: Location, measured variable and scope of the supplied evidence.

diagrams.title: Aggregation can conceal neighbourhood contrast
diagrams.description: The combined rate lies between sharply different local rates.

edges.label: form an average that hides the contrast

lessons.summary: Analyse a public choice through feasible alternatives, opportunity cost, spatial access and evidence about affected groups.
objectives: Identify the next-best feasible alternative.
Calculate a budget trade-off with explicit units.
Evaluate distribution without treating price as social value.
explanation: Economic choice arises when limited resources have competing uses. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone, not the sum of all rejected options. A budget describes affordability under stated prices and constraints; it does not tell us which option best serves a community. Identify the decision-maker, the resource and the realistic alternatives before comparing outcomes.

An integrated inquiry also asks where benefits and costs fall and how earlier decisions shape the choices available now. A service can have a low operating cost yet be difficult for some people to reach. A historically neglected area may have different needs from an already well-served area, but that description requires evidence. Separate measured effects, stakeholder priorities and a reasoned value judgement. All cases here are hypothetical and do not recommend an actual public spending decision.
keyIdeas: Opportunity cost concerns the best rejected alternative.
Affordability differs from desirability.
Location and past provision affect access.

definitions.meaning: The value of the next-best feasible alternative given up by a decision.
The limit on affordable combinations imposed by the available budget and prices.
How benefits or costs differ among people, groups or places.

method: Identify the scarce resource and feasible choices.
State the next-best alternative forgone.
Calculate relevant costs or trade-offs under explicit assumptions.
Compare access, prior provision and effects across groups.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical council has 24,000 credits for equipment only. Benches cost 600 credits each and noticeboards 1,200 credits each at fixed prices. With the whole budget spent on these two goods, find the bench trade-off for one extra noticeboard.
steps: One noticeboard costs 1,200/600 = 2 benches.
The budget could buy 40 benches alone or 20 noticeboards alone.
Replacing two benches with one noticeboard keeps spending unchanged at a feasible combination.
workedExample.conclusion: One extra noticeboard forgoes two benches in this model. Which option has greater public value needs evidence about use, location and priorities.

misconceptions.mistake: Calling the purchase price the whole social opportunity cost.
misconceptions.correction: Consider the best alternative use and its forgone benefits.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming the cheapest option gives equal access.
misconceptions.correction: Check location, eligibility and users’ circumstances.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical fixed budget is fully spent on two services. One workshop costs 180 credits and one reading session 60 credits. Calculate the session trade-off for one extra workshop.
hints: Compare costs in alternative units.
solution: 180/60 = 3 reading sessions per workshop.
One extra workshop requires giving up three sessions under these assumptions.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical council selects a park instead of a clinic. The clinic was its next-best feasible use of the same land. State the opportunity cost and identify one spatial question for evaluation.
hints: Distinguish alternative benefits from the selected project’s bill.
solution: The opportunity cost is the value of the clinic’s forgone benefits.
A relevant spatial question is which residents would lose convenient clinic access compared with existing provision.
The case does not quantify those benefits or establish which project is preferable.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical proposal closes two local study rooms and opens one larger room at lower total operating cost. Evaluate whether lower cost alone establishes success.
hints: Consider capacity and who can reach the service.
solution: Lower operating cost supports a cost-saving claim on that boundary.
Capacity, opening hours, travel time and access for different users may change.
Compare those outcomes and any transition costs with the policy’s stated objectives before judging success.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical programme A costs 9000 credits for 450 sessions; B costs 7200 for 300. Find cost per session and identify the lower figure.
hints: Divide each cost by its sessions.
Do not compare total cost alone.
solution: A costs 20 credits per session; B costs 24.
A has the lower unit cost even though its total cost is greater.

practice.prompt: A free public event uses staff time that would otherwise run the next-best feasible reading programme. Does zero ticket price mean no opportunity cost?
hints: Public resources are still used.
Identify the forgone alternative.
solution: The event uses scarce staff time even without charging attendees.
Its opportunity cost includes the benefit of the reading programme forgone under the stated choice.

checklist: I state price and budget assumptions.
I separate facts and value judgements.

notes.title: Unit cost is one decision criterion
paragraphs: Public choices involve opportunity costs even when no direct fee is charged to users. A fixed budget allocated to one service leaves less for another, while a land-use decision can constrain future options for many years. Cost-effectiveness compares resources used for a specified outcome; it is not the same as overall fairness or value. A cheaper central facility may serve more people per credit while imposing longer journeys on outlying residents. Evaluate both the measurable trade-off and the distribution of benefits and burdens. State the next-best feasible alternative rather than listing every imaginable use of resources.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical council compares mobile outreach costing 6000 credits for 300 visits with a central service costing 8000 for 500 visits. Compare cost per visit and a limitation.
steps: Outreach costs 6000/300 = 20 credits per visit; central service costs 8000/500 = 16.
The central service is cheaper per recorded visit.
workedExamples.conclusion: The measure does not establish equal quality or access for residents unable to travel centrally.

flashcards.front: What is cost-effectiveness?
flashcards.back: Resource cost relative to a specified outcome.

flashcards.front: Does lowest cost per user establish fairness?
flashcards.back: No; access and distribution may differ.

flashcards.front: What is a public project’s opportunity cost?
flashcards.back: The value of the next-best feasible use of its resources.

flashcards.front: Why define the service outcome?
flashcards.back: Different quality or benefits make raw cost comparisons misleading.

diagrams.title: Unit cost is one decision criterion
diagrams.description: A lower cost per visit can coexist with different access outcomes.

nodes.label: Decision context
nodes.detail: Compare quality and who can reach each service

lessons.summary: Trace connections across places and time while distinguishing a transmission mechanism from a guaranteed outcome.
objectives: Identify stocks, flows and system boundaries.
Trace a disruption through connected activities.
Evaluate adaptation and unequal effects.
explanation: A system is a set of connected parts considered within a stated boundary. Global systems link places through material, financial, information and human flows. A supply network can include several production stages and alternative routes. Define which actors and connections an explanation includes, and distinguish an amount held at a date from a flow over time. A diagram is a selective model, not a complete description of the world.

A change in one part can affect others through a stated mechanism, but the size and timing depend on stocks, contracts, alternatives and responses. Historical evidence can explain how a network developed, while geographical evidence locates exposure to disruption and economic evidence identifies incentives to adapt. Do not assume a local disruption must produce an identical global effect. The hypothetical cases here hold some conditions fixed to make a mechanism assessable; actual outcomes require further evidence.
keyIdeas: Define the system boundary.
Trace each step of a mechanism.
Stocks and alternatives can change timing and impact.

definitions.meaning: The line defining which components and connections an analysis includes.
A transfer of material, money, information or people over a period.
The capacity of a system to cope with disruption while maintaining or restoring relevant functions.

method: Identify components, locations and included flows.
Trace the proposed change through a sequence of links.
Check stocks, alternatives and possible responses.
Evaluate who is affected and what remains uncertain.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical workshop has 240 components in stock and uses 30 per day at a constant rate. A delivery is delayed; no components arrive during the delay. How long can the stock support production at that rate?
steps: Stock is 240 components; use is a flow of 30 components per day.
Coverage = 240/30 = 8 days.
After eight full days the model stock is zero; continued production then requires new supply or changed use.
workedExample.conclusion: The stock supports eight days at the stated rate. This does not establish the delay’s length or the wider network’s total loss.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a diagram’s omitted connections as nonexistent.
misconceptions.correction: State that the boundary is selective and check relevant external links.

misconceptions.mistake: Assuming every linked actor suffers the same effect.
misconceptions.correction: Examine contracts, stocks, substitutes and distribution.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical producer holds 150 units and uses 25 units per day, with no deliveries or other losses. Calculate stock coverage.
hints: Divide stock by daily use.
solution: Coverage = 150/25 = 6 days at the constant rate.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical supplier cannot send packaging to a food producer for three days. The producer has five days of packaging stock at its unchanged production rate. Explain why an immediate production stop does not follow.
hints: Distinguish the delayed flow from the available stock.
solution: Existing packaging stock can support the three-day interval under the stated conditions.
The five-day coverage exceeds the three-day delay.
This does not rule out other costs or constraints, but the packaging delay alone does not force an immediate stop.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical network relies on one transport route. A proposal adds a second route at higher operating cost. Evaluate the resilience claim without assuming it must succeed.
hints: Are the routes exposed to the same disruption?
solution: A usable alternative could preserve flows when one route fails.
Shared hazards, inadequate capacity or delays in switching could limit that benefit.
Compare route independence, capacity, switching time and costs against the required service before judging the proposal.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical serial line has stage capacities 40, 65 and 55 units/hour. Find its maximum steady output and the new limit if the first stage rises to 60.
hints: Use the smallest capacity each time.
The bottleneck can move.
solution: Initially the limit is 40 units/hour.
After the first stage rises to 60, the smallest capacity is 55, so the new limit is 55 units/hour.

practice.prompt: A firm doubles warehouse stock but keeps one irreplaceable supplier. Does the extra stock eliminate supplier risk?
hints: A buffer covers only a finite interval.
Replacement capacity remains unchanged.
solution: More stock can delay the effect of a disruption.
A sufficiently long supplier failure can still exhaust it, so the single-source dependency remains.

checklist: I test alternatives and unequal effects.

notes.title: The smallest stage capacity limits a serial system
paragraphs: A production network can be limited by a bottleneck: the stage with the lowest usable capacity when every finished item must pass through all stages. Increasing capacity elsewhere may not increase final output until the bottleneck changes. Networks also contain buffers, alternative routes and shared dependencies, so the effect of one disruption depends on the whole arrangement. A stock can delay interruption but does not provide indefinite resilience. Use consistent units and service periods when comparing capacities, and distinguish a theoretical maximum from actual output affected by quality, downtime and demand.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical production line can prepare 80 units/day, assemble 50 and pack 70. Every unit passes through all stages. Find the maximum steady output without stocks between stages.
steps: Assembly is the smallest capacity at 50 units/day.
The line’s steady output is therefore limited to 50 units/day.
workedExamples.conclusion: Raising preparation to 100 alone would not remove the assembly bottleneck.

flashcards.front: What is a bottleneck?
flashcards.back: The capacity-limiting stage in a linked process.

flashcards.front: Can improving a non-bottleneck raise final output automatically?
flashcards.back: No; the limiting stage may remain unchanged.

flashcards.front: What does a buffer stock do?
flashcards.back: It can absorb temporary differences or delays.

flashcards.front: Why compare capacities over the same period?
flashcards.back: Otherwise the rates are not directly comparable.

diagrams.title: The smallest stage capacity limits a serial system
diagrams.description: Every completed unit must pass through assembly.

lessons.summary: Evaluate a sustainability decision using comparable services, time horizons and evidence about who bears costs.
objectives: Define an assessment boundary and service.
Calculate a simple resource comparison.
Integrate environmental and social evidence in a qualified judgement.
explanation: A sustainability inquiry asks whether an activity can meet needs while maintaining conditions needed in the future. Make the question assessable by defining the service, place, timescale and relevant impacts. A comparison should consider equivalent service and include the stages it claims to cover. A lower use-stage resource requirement does not by itself establish a better whole-life result.

Combine the environmental account with evidence about affordability, access and the distribution of costs. Historical decisions may have locked in infrastructure or created unequal access, so a proposal’s starting point matters. Do not collapse unlike outcomes into a single score without explaining weights and assumptions. A judgement can favour an option conditionally while identifying a cost borne by a particular group. The hypothetical exercises below illustrate this reasoning; their simplified resource figures are not real product assessments.
keyIdeas: Compare equivalent services.
State included stages and time horizon.
A qualified judgement can recognise both gains and burdens.

definitions.meaning: The processes, impacts, places and time period included in a comparison.
A defined amount of service used as a common basis for comparing options.
A choice in which benefits and burdens fall differently across groups or places.

method: Specify the service and the question being judged.
Set the stages, impacts and time horizon.
Calculate comparable quantities without combining unlike units.
Integrate access and distribution evidence in a conditional conclusion.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical classroom model compares one drinking-container use. A disposable container requires 1 litre of water to make. A reusable container requires 20 litres to make plus 0.2 litres to wash after each use. Ignore all other water use; both provide equivalent service. After how many uses is reusable water use lower?
steps: After n uses, disposable water use is n litres; reusable use is 20 + 0.2n litres.
Reusable is lower when 20 + 0.2n < n, so n > 25.
At 25 uses both use 25 litres; at 26 uses reusable uses 25.2 litres and disposable 26 litres.
workedExample.conclusion: The reusable option is lower from 26 whole uses under this boundary. This calculation does not establish overall environmental superiority or actual reuse behaviour.

misconceptions.correction: Check whether the question asks for equal use or lower use.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating one resource measure as a complete sustainability verdict.
misconceptions.correction: Consider other impacts, lifetime and access on stated boundaries.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical service provides 500 equivalent uses. Option A consumes 3 litres per use; B consumes 2 litres per use, counting the use stage only. Calculate each total and B’s saving.
hints: Multiply each intensity by the same service amount.
solution: A uses 1,500 litres; B uses 1,000 litres.
B saves 500 litres at the use stage for these 500 uses.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical town replaces free water refill points with paid machines that use less electricity per litre. Identify one environmental claim supported by the description and one access question it leaves unresolved.
hints: Separate per-litre energy from who can obtain water.
solution: The machines have lower electricity intensity per litre under the stated comparison.
Whether residents who cannot afford the charge retain adequate access is unresolved.
Total energy also depends on litres delivered, and other life-cycle impacts are not supplied.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical plan reduces bus fuel use per passenger-kilometre but removes evening services used by shift workers. Develop a qualified judgement using both facts.
hints: Which objective improves and which group may lose access?
solution: Fuel intensity improves under the stated measure.
Removing evening services reduces the available service for the specified users; the size of their resulting travel burden needs evidence.
Support for the plan should depend on total impacts and an adequate access alternative, rather than intensity alone.

practice.prompt: A hypothetical repair scheme reduces discarded items from 250 to 175 per month. Find the reduction and percentage change.
hints: Subtract final from initial for the reduction.
Use the initial 250 as denominator.
solution: Reduction = 75 items per month.
Percentage reduction = 75/250 × 100% = 30%.

practice.prompt: A plan predicts 20% lower electricity use, but no post-installation readings exist. How should the claim be reported?
hints: A model estimate differs from a measured outcome.
Specify the evidence needed for verification.
solution: Report a projected 20% reduction under the plan’s assumptions.
Compare consistent before-and-after metered use, accounting for service levels and other changes, before claiming the saving occurred.

notes.title: One intervention can improve a metric and create an access issue
paragraphs: A sustainability judgement should connect environmental, social and economic outcomes rather than collapse them into one unexplained score. Some improvements can be measured directly, such as reduced water use for the same service; others involve distribution, access or long-term maintenance. Trade-offs should be made visible so affected groups can understand whose interests are prioritised. A target also needs a baseline and a time horizon. Avoid counting a projected saving as an observed result before implementation. Compare actual use with the assumptions behind the plan and revise the judgement when demand, durability or access differs from expectations.

workedExamples.prompt: Hypothetical refill scheme reduces disposable bottles from 1000 to 600 per month, but moves all refill stations to a distant central building. Evaluate two outcomes.
steps: Bottle use falls by 400, or 40%, supporting the stated reduction outcome.
Centralisation may worsen access for people far from the building; journey and usage evidence is needed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The environmental measure improves, but overall success depends on access and other impacts.

flashcards.front: What should a sustainability target include?
flashcards.back: A defined outcome, baseline and timescale.

flashcards.front: Why separate projections from results?
flashcards.back: An expected saving has not yet been observed.

flashcards.front: What is a distributional question?
flashcards.back: Who receives benefits and who bears costs or barriers.

flashcards.front: How should trade-offs be reported?
flashcards.back: Explicitly, with the criteria and affected groups identified.

diagrams.title: One intervention can improve a metric and create an access issue
diagrams.description: A narrower outcome must be connected to wider service consequences.

nodes.label: Access question
nodes.detail: Longer journeys may exclude some users

lessons.summary: Compare supported viewpoints in context without inventing motives or treating every claim as equally evidenced.
objectives: Identify what a source explicitly values.
Distinguish viewpoint from factual accuracy.
Compare perspectives while preserving context and uncertainty.
explanation: A perspective is a way of interpreting an issue shaped by experience, position, values and available information. Identify it through specific evidence in a source, rather than assuming everyone in a group thinks alike. A person can offer useful evidence while having an interest in the outcome. Conversely, an apparently neutral tone does not establish accuracy. Evaluate each factual claim through its method and corroboration.

Historical perspective also requires attention to the conditions and information available at the time, rather than attributing present knowledge to past actors. Understanding a viewpoint does not require endorsing it. When comparing contemporary stakeholders, distinguish disagreements about facts from disagreements about priorities. The short statements below are original fictional teaching texts, not quotations from actual people or archival documents. Their wording supports limited interpretations; do not invent biography, hidden motives or a consensus for an entire group.
keyIdeas: Ground perspective in specific wording.
Understanding does not imply endorsement.
Different priorities do not make every factual claim equally supported.

definitions.meaning: A way of interpreting an issue shaped by a person’s position, experience, values and information.
Testing a claim against other relevant evidence, while checking independence.
Interpreting past people as if they necessarily had present-day knowledge or assumptions.

method: Identify the source, context and exact claim.
Use specific words to infer stated priorities.
Compare factual claims separately from value priorities.
Corroborate and identify limits before generalising.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical consultation contains two fictional statements about a proposed market square: trader, “I need delivery access before opening”; resident, “I want space where children can play after school.” Compare their stated priorities.
steps: The trader’s statement prioritises delivery access before business opens.
The resident’s statement prioritises play space after school.
Different time periods may permit a shared arrangement, but feasibility is not established by the statements.
workedExample.conclusion: The priorities differ without necessarily being incompatible. Neither speaker can be assumed to represent every trader or resident.

misconceptions.mistake: Assigning one speaker’s view to an entire group.
misconceptions.correction: State the source’s scope and seek broader evidence.

misconceptions.mistake: Inventing motives to explain a disagreement.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical fictional statement from a commuter: “Keep the early train; my shift starts before the buses run.” Infer one priority and support it with a detail.
hints: Connect the requested service to the stated timing.
solution: The speaker prioritises transport that fits an early work shift.
The detail that the shift starts before buses run supports the need for the early train.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical fictional statements: planner, “The route should carry the greatest number of riders”; resident, “The route should still reach our isolated street.” Compare priorities without inventing either speaker’s motives.
hints: Separate total ridership from geographic inclusion.
solution: The planner prioritises total ridership.
The resident prioritises service reaching an isolated location.
The statements reveal different evaluation criteria; they do not establish hostility, selfishness or the optimal route.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical fictional 1900 letter says its author expects a new rail line to increase local trade. A student says the author must have known the line would close in 1950. Evaluate the student’s inference; no other evidence is supplied.
hints: What information was available at the time of writing?
solution: The letter supports an expectation of increased trade, not knowledge of a later closure.
Later outcomes cannot be assigned to the author’s knowledge without contemporary evidence.
The claim imports hindsight; investigate information available in 1900 before explaining the expectation.

practice.prompt: Fictional school consultation is held during the only bus home for rural pupils. Identify a possible missing perspective and an improvement.
hints: Timing can exclude a group.
Provide another accessible way to contribute.
solution: Rural pupils relying on that bus may be underrepresented.
Offer a different time or an accessible alternative response method so their views can be included.

practice.prompt: A fictional report quotes one shopkeeper against a pedestrian zone and concludes all businesses oppose it. Explain the inference problem.
hints: One person does not represent every business.
Different locations and activities may create different interests.
solution: The quotation supports that shopkeeper’s stated view.
Other businesses may have different delivery, customer and access needs, so wider evidence is required for an all-business claim.

checklist: I avoid invented motives and group claims.

notes.title: Participation shapes the recorded perspective
paragraphs: Consultation records show the views of participants, not automatically those of an entire community. Attendance, language, timing and confidence can influence who speaks. A quiet or absent group should not be assumed to agree. Stakeholder analysis identifies interests and possible effects while avoiding the assumption that everyone within a category shares one view. Evaluate a proposal using both reported priorities and evidence about consequences. A fair account can recognise conflicting needs without inventing motives or treating the loudest voice as the most representative. Explain how missing perspectives would be sought and how uncertainty affects the judgement.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional consultation: an evening meeting records support for a park plan from 18 attendees, while the invitation reached only one housing block. Assess representativeness.
steps: The result shows support among the people who attended from the contacted group.
It does not establish town-wide support because other blocks and non-attendees are missing.
workedExamples.conclusion: Broader outreach at varied times and through accessible formats would improve coverage.

flashcards.front: Does silence imply agreement?
flashcards.back: No; absence or non-participation has several possible causes.

flashcards.front: What is a stakeholder?
flashcards.back: A person or group affected by or able to influence a decision.

flashcards.front: Can one stakeholder category contain different views?
flashcards.back: Yes.

flashcards.front: Why assess consultation coverage?
flashcards.back: Participation determines whose perspectives are represented.

diagrams.title: Participation shapes the recorded perspective
diagrams.description: A consultation result inherits the limits of who was reached and attended.

lessons.summary: Build an integrated argument that weighs different measures and groups, preserves source limits and answers the inquiry.
objectives: Form a thesis supported by the supplied packet.
Connect disciplinary evidence through reasoning.
Qualify a judgement when outcomes differ across groups.
explanation: An extended response should answer a focused question through a defensible argument. Define the outcome being judged, choose evidence relevant to it and explain why that evidence supports the claim. Integration means showing how different perspectives change the conclusion, not simply placing a geography paragraph beside an economics paragraph. Distinguish an observed change from evidence that a particular policy caused it.

Plan around claims and counterevidence. Preserve the units, dates, populations and source limitations when combining data. A mean improvement can coexist with deterioration for a subgroup, while a cost saving can coexist with weaker access. State how those tensions affect the judgement and what further evidence would resolve uncertainty. The fictional packets below are complete for each task; use their supplied information rather than inventing historical context, stakeholder motives or unreported outcomes. Alternative responses can satisfy the criteria when precisely supported.
keyIdeas: A thesis must fit the evidence supplied.
Synthesis explains why combined evidence changes the judgement.
Limits should shape the conclusion.

definitions.meaning: The central, arguable answer that a response develops and supports.
A reasoned integration of evidence or perspectives that explains their combined implications.
A condition or limit that narrows a claim to what the evidence supports.

method: Define the question and evaluation criteria.
Group evidence by claims and tensions.
Explain how combined evidence supports or limits each claim.
Conclude with a qualified answer and targeted evidence needs.

workedExample.prompt: Hypothetical packet follows the same 100 travellers before and after a route change, using the same method: 80 central residents’ mean trip falls from 20 to 15 minutes; 20 outer residents’ mean rises from 30 to 35 minutes. Judge whether measured travel improved for everyone.
steps: Initial overall mean = (80 × 20 + 20 × 30)/100 = 22 minutes.
Later mean = (80 × 15 + 20 × 35)/100 = 19 minutes.
The overall mean falls by 3 minutes, while the outer group’s mean rises by 5 minutes. These group means do not identify every individual change.
workedExample.conclusion: Measured average travel time improves overall but not for both groups on average, so improvement for everyone is unsupported. Before-and-after data alone do not isolate the route change’s causal effect.

misconceptions.mistake: Repeating a statistic without explaining its relevance.
misconceptions.correction: Link it to the inquiry and state its limits.

misconceptions.mistake: Ending with a universal verdict despite mixed evidence.
misconceptions.correction: Qualify the answer by group, measure and causal uncertainty.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical packet: a library’s weekly visits rise after later opening hours begin, while its electricity bill rises too. Write a thesis about whether the change succeeded, using only these facts.
hints: Define which outcomes improved and what cannot yet be judged.
solution: Visits increased, but the higher electricity bill creates a cost trade-off; overall success depends on the library’s access and budget objectives.
The timing alone does not prove that later hours caused the entire visits increase.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical packet uses comparable definitions: average bus fare falls from 4 to 3 credits, but a remote neighbourhood loses its only bus route. Explain how the evidence changes an evaluation focused on access.
hints: Price matters only where usable service exists.
solution: Average fare falls by 1 credit, or 25% relative to 4 credits.
The remote neighbourhood loses bus-route access despite that average price reduction.
An access judgement must consider both affordability and service geography; lower average fares do not establish universal improvement.

practice.prompt: Hypothetical packet: a council publicity leaflet claims a new square benefits all residents; a convenience sample of ten nearby shopkeepers reports higher sales. Evaluate the support for the universal claim and propose two useful additional sources.
hints: Who and what are missing from these sources?
solution: The leaflet states the council’s claim; the shopkeeper sample concerns reported sales among a small selected group.
Neither establishes benefits for all residents, and the two sources may not be independent if the leaflet uses that same survey.
A transparently sampled resident survey could test access and experience across neighbourhoods; comparable records of use, costs and displacement could test other outcomes.

practice.prompt: Fictional packet: a market renovation increases stall capacity but rent rises beyond some former traders’ budgets. Write a qualified thesis about opportunity for traders.
hints: Capacity and affordability are different dimensions.
Use both facts in the judgement.
solution: Possible thesis: The renovation expanded physical trading capacity, but higher rents limited access for some former traders.
The judgement distinguishes more spaces from affordable opportunities and avoids claiming every trader benefited.

practice.prompt: A fictional essay dismisses interview evidence of a closed footpath because a townwide average journey time improved. Explain a stronger use of both sources.
hints: Averages and particular barriers address different scales.
Neither automatically invalidates the other.
solution: The average supports an overall measured time improvement within its population.
The interview can reveal a local access cost hidden by that average; the conclusion should recognise both and examine the path’s affected users.

notes.title: A judgement must include unequal outcomes
paragraphs: An extended response should use its evidence to answer a question, not merely describe each source in turn. Organise paragraphs around criteria or claims, then connect quantitative patterns with relevant experiences and context. A counterargument should be addressed with evidence or used to qualify the judgement. Distinguish improvement in a mean from improvement for every group. If sources are limited, state the narrow conclusion they support and identify what remains unresolved. A strong final judgement weighs the most relevant outcomes explicitly, showing why some evidence carries more weight for the stated question without concealing conflicting findings.

workedExamples.prompt: Fictional packet: a cycle route reduces average journey time from 24 to 18 minutes among surveyed cyclists; wheelchair users report blocked crossings at two locations. Judge transport accessibility.
steps: Cyclists’ mean time falls by 6 minutes, or 25%, showing a measured benefit for that sample.
Blocked crossings indicate a distinct access barrier for wheelchair users.
workedExamples.conclusion: Accessibility improved for the surveyed cyclists but cannot be judged universally better without resolving the reported barriers.

flashcards.front: How should extended-response paragraphs be organised?
flashcards.back: Around analytical claims or criteria relevant to the question.

flashcards.front: What role should counter-evidence play?
flashcards.back: Test or qualify the judgement.

flashcards.front: Does a better mean prove everyone improved?
flashcards.back: No; distributional outcomes can differ.

flashcards.front: What makes a final judgement transparent?
flashcards.back: Explicitly weighing evidence against stated criteria.

diagrams.title: A judgement must include unequal outcomes
diagrams.description: A measured average benefit does not erase a separate barrier.
